problem: Prior floor-plan-guided navigation methods assume accurate, metrically faithful maps and fail on imprecise hand-drawn sketch maps that are sparse, simplified and distorted. There was also no benchmark for navigating unseen environments from sketch maps alone.
motivation: People often give directions by sketching a route map, which is fast to produce and needs no GPS or precise floor plan. An agent must align sparse, distorted sketches with its own egocentric view and the map it builds on-site. The paper argues that patch-based encoders handle sparse strokes poorly, so a geometry-aware descriptor and explicit sketch-to-exploration-map alignment are needed.
key_idea: Encode sketch and exploration maps as ray-based descriptors over keypoints, then use cross-attention between the two maps to predict the goal position, which is fed to an RL navigation policy.
insight: Explicit dual-map alignment matters more than simply feeding the maps to a CNN. Adding an exploration map with a plain CNN gives only modest gains (SR 5.6→8.6 on Low val-unseen), whereas adding DAGP gives a further 3.6–5.3 SR points (8.6→12.7 Low, 3.9→8.0 High val-unseen). RGB hurts, likely because texture and colour cues are absent from sketches and act as noise. Visualisations show goal predictions converging as the explored area grows.
method: SoR dataset pipeline: builds occupancy maps from Matterport3D, denoises them (erosion, largest connected component), samples start/goal pairs with A*, crops the trajectory-related region, then renders Low-abstraction (polygon contours) and High-abstraction (CLIPasso Bézier-curve sketches) maps, followed by manual verification.

Ray-based Map Descriptor (RMD): samples a 9x9 lattice of keypoints per map and casts N=8 rays from each. Each keypoint is described by normalised obstacle distances plus its (x,y) coordinates, giving a dense feature for sparse sketches.

Dual-Map Aligned Goal Predictor (DAGP): applies self-attention to the sketch RMD and the exploration-map RMD (a learnable goal embedding is added to the sketch keypoint nearest the goal). Cross-attention with exploration features as queries, then an MLP and softmax, gives per-keypoint goal probabilities. The goal is the probability-weighted average of the keypoint coordinates.
Policy: CNN encoders for depth, exploration map (built as in ESC) and sketch. Their features and the estimated goal feed a GRU (hidden size 512), followed by a softmax over STOP/FORWARD/LEFT/RIGHT.
Training: PPO plus lambda*L2 goal regression (lambda=1). Reward is a shaped sum of geodesic-distance reduction (2.0), imitation of the shortest-path expert action (0.05) and success (10.0).

setting.backbone: CNN encoders + 2-layer attention DAGP + GRU policy (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: SoR: 54,774 sketch-trajectory pairs over 71 Matterport3D scenes (auto-generated sketches plus some human-drawn ones in the validation set)
setting.observation: egocentric depth, on-site built top-down exploration map, and the sketch map with start and goal markers
setting.action_space: discrete low-level: STOP, MOVE FORWARD, TURN LEFT, TURN RIGHT
setting.privileged: none at test time (GT goal is used only as a training supervision target); the sketch marks start and goal

numbers_note: SoR is the paper's own benchmark, so the 'other:' names are used, one per abstraction level. The numbers are copied from Table 1.
results: SkeNavigator beats the adapted FloDiff baseline on all four SoR validation sets. On High val-unseen SPL is 7.6 vs 3.8, roughly the claimed 105% relative gain. On Low val-unseen SR is 12.7 vs 3.9. Humans reach 94–100% SR, so the gap to human performance remains very large.
limitations: Absolute success rates are low (8–17% SR), far below human performance (94–100%).
Most sketches are synthetically generated (Bézier / polygon style transfer); only a small human-drawn subset is used for validation.
Evaluated only in simulation (Matterport3D) with a single adapted baseline (FloDiff); no real-robot tests.
